primary_topics: Chapter 8 of 'Judicial Renaissance' -- a keynote address to an ADB-sponsored symposium arguing that access to justice, especially by the poor, is as essential to good governance and economic development as investor confidence.

The opening of the 'judicial fortress': the Court's historic image as a Mount Olympus of unapproachable gods, and the transparency now demanded of it by the Constitution, the ethics codes, the information revolution and a persistent media.

A three-tier demonstration of the Philippine legal order's pro-poor bias -- a Constitution that is pro-poor, pro-labor and pro-human rights; congressional legislation implementing those mandates; and Supreme Court measures and decisions opening the justice system to indigents.

The Court's social-justice jurisprudence in practice: the party-list ruling in Ang Bagong Bayani, eight settled labor doctrines, human-rights safeguards in criminal procedure, and strict review of death sentences culminating in People v. Mateo -- all defended against business and diplomatic criticism.
sub_topics: CJP recalls that at the 9th Conference of Chief Justices in Christchurch, New Zealand on October 4-8, 2001, UN and World Bank speakers praised the Philippine Court's efforts on judicial independence and integrity, an unsolicited tribute he heard with pride.

He inventories subsequent endorsements: the World Bank posting the APJR blueprint on its website as a model, USAID, CIDA and AusAID assistance on computerization and transparency, advanced Japanese negotiations for the Tagaytay Philja complex, a 2.3-million-euro EU grant for Access to Justice for the Poor, and ADB TA No. 3693-PHI.
He describes the highest court of the past as shrouded in mystery -- a fortress, a Mount Olympus where the gods were unapproachable and untouchable.

Despite that mystery the Court is coequal with the President and Congress and is vested with the duty to nullify any governmental act for grave abuse of discretion, having struck down laws, executive and administrative orders and mega-contracts.
The judiciary's role reaches almost every aspect of national and community life and stands as the last bulwark of democracy and the ultimate recourse of the people in redressing grievances.

The growing call for transparency has partly opened the fortress doors: the Constitution, the Ethical Standards Law, the Canons of Judicial Ethics and the New Code of Judicial Conduct have invaded the judicial enclave, and media have penetrated its thick walls.

Development agencies such as the World Bank and ADB attend to the judiciary because stability in the rule of law and predictability of decisions are indispensable to investor confidence, economic development and good governance.

ADB General Counsel Arthur M. Mitchell's invitation letter asked him to address how an effective and accountable judiciary reduces poverty by leveling the economic playing field, providing access to opportunity, food and shelter, and protecting substantive and procedural due process.
Given only twenty minutes, he says he will speak in broad bullet-type strokes with detailed footnotes in the distributed hard copy.

First, the 1987 Constitution, arising from the ashes of an authoritarian regime, is international in outlook, promotive of social justice, respectful of human rights, responsive to women, protective of labor and cognizant of indigenous cultural communities, guaranteeing free access to courts and legal assistance not to be denied by reason of poverty.

Second, Congress has implemented those mandates with laws on the rights of arrested persons, domestic violence, child protection, human rights violations, barangay dispute settlement, low-cost housing, agriculture and small farmers, and protection to labor.

Third, the Court itself has opened the system to indigents by exempting them from docket fees and transcript costs, protecting the constitutional rights of the accused, granting free counsel and requiring lawyers to represent poor litigants, supplemented by IBP and FLAG pro bono work and the Shari'ah Appellate Court established under RA 6734.

In Ang Bagong Bayani-OFW Labor Party v. Comelec, which he penned, the Court held the party-list system reserved for the marginalized -- to give them not only genuine hope but genuine power and a direct voice in Congress.

The Court's pro-poor bias is clearest in labor law, continuing the seeds sown in 1940 by Calalang v. Williams, and expressed in eight enumerated doctrines from just-cause-and-due-process dismissal to the non-binding character of quitclaims and liability of local recruiters for OFW contracts.

In human rights the Court has penalized judges who failed to inform uneducated accused of their right to counsel, annulled judgments lacking a 'searching inquiry' on guilty pleas, voided judgments failing constitutional form and substance, and extended the Universal Declaration of Human Rights to everyone including aliens.

On the death penalty -- declared constitutional despite his own unyielding personal opinion that it was not -- the Court has affirmed less than one third of death sentences and in People v. Mateo required Court of Appeals review of all death and life sentences, with conforming amendments to Rules 122 and 124.

He acknowledges the criticism this draws: guilty parties acquitted on stringent evidentiary requirements and the inadmissibility of illegally obtained evidence, and businessmen complaining that labor law hampers discipline of erring employees.

He answers that the judiciary must keep its social justice orientation because the Constitution and laws require it, and because the marginalized, if denied access to the democratic institutions of justice, may be tempted to take the law into their own hands.

He closes by quoting his own book 'Leveling the Playing Field' on the Court safeguarding food and freedom, jobs and justice, indulgences and integrity, development and democracy, prosperity and peace, and congratulates the ADB for its interest in the nexus between justice and development.

stances.claim: Access to justice, especially by the poor, is as essential to good governance as investor confidence in the economy, because stability in the rule of law and predictability in the rendition of decisions are indispensable to development.
stances.rhetorical_move: yoking the poverty agenda to the investor agenda so that a development-bank audience hears access to justice as economic infrastructure rather than charity

stances.claim: The judiciary can no longer operate as a fortress: transparency requirements of the Constitution and the ethics codes, the information revolution and the media have rightly invaded the judicial enclave, and people no longer accept doctrines they do not understand or judgments resting on unexplained rationale.
stances.rhetorical_move: sustained fortress-and-Mount-Olympus metaphor, narrated as a siege the Court has accepted and should accept

stances.claim: The Philippine Supreme Court has been openly and unabashedly pro-poor, pro-labor and pro-human rights, as shown by its indigent-access measures, its party-list ruling, its settled labor doctrines and its criminal-procedure safeguards.
stances.rhetorical_move: three-tier proof from Constitution to statute to jurisprudence, with named cases and an eight-point doctrinal list supplying the evidence

stances.claim: The judiciary must keep its social justice orientation despite criticism from businessmen and foreign observers, because the Constitution and laws require it and because the marginalized, if denied access to democratic institutions of justice, may take the law into their own hands.
stances.rhetorical_move: concede-the-criticism-then-answer-it, closing with a consequentialist warning about what denial of access produces

stances.claim: The death penalty was declared constitutional by the Court despite his own unyielding personal opinion that it was not, and death convicts must be given the same opportunity for multiple review as those convicted of lesser crimes.
stances.rhetorical_move: separating his personal dissenting conviction from the institution's holding, then pressing the procedural remedy the Court did adopt

notable_anecdotes: CJP recalls sitting at the 9th Conference of Chief Justices in Christchurch in October 2001 and hearing UN and World Bank speakers praise the Philippine Supreme Court, saying he was 'singularly proud' as a Filipino citizen to hear that unsolicited tribute.
He quotes ADB General Counsel Arthur M. Mitchell's invitation letter, which set the terms of the address by asking him to show how a more effective and accountable judiciary reduces poverty.
He notes that he was given only twenty minutes, so he would speak in broad bullet-type strokes while supplying detailed footnotes in the hard copy to be distributed afterwards.

He recalls the lament of a foreign diplomat who wryly commented that in his country -- unlike in the Philippines -- no guilty person, rich or poor, had ever been acquitted on a mere technicality of the law.

He discloses that the death penalty was upheld as constitutional 'despite my unyielding personal opinion that it was not,' and that he quotes his own earlier book 'Leveling the Playing Field' for the summation of the Court's balancing role.

one_paragraph_summary: Chapter 8 of 'Judicial Renaissance' reproduces the keynote address Justice Panganiban delivered at an Asian Development Bank symposium on judicial reforms, on the theme of enhancing the effectiveness and accountability of the judiciary. He began by recalling the 9th Conference of Chief Justices in Christchurch in October 2001, where UN and World Bank speakers praised the Philippine Supreme Court, and listed the endorsements that followed: the World Bank posting the Action Program for Judicial Reform on its website as a model, assistance from USAID, CIDA and AusAID, advanced negotiations for a Japanese grant to build the Philippine Judicial Academy complex in Tagaytay, a 2.3-million-euro European Union grant for Access to Justice for the Poor, and ADB TA No. 3693-PHI on strengthening independence and defining accountability. He described the highest court of the past as a fortress, a Mount Olympus whose gods were unapproachable, and argued that transparency requirements of the Constitution, the Ethical Standards Law and the judicial conduct codes, together with the information revolution and a persistent media, had partly opened its doors -- a development he accepted, since people no longer accept doctrines they do not understand. Answering ADB General Counsel Arthur M. Mitchell's invitation to show how an accountable judiciary reduces poverty, he made a three-tier case: the 1987 Constitution is pro-poor, pro-labor and pro-human rights and guarantees legal assistance that shall not be denied by reason of poverty; Congress has passed implementing laws on arrest rights, domestic violence, child protection, barangay dispute settlement, housing, agriculture and labor; and the Court itself exempts indigents from fees, grants free counsel, works with the IBP and FLAG, and authorized the Shari'ah Appellate Court. He cited his own ponencia in Ang Bagong Bayani reserving the party-list system for the marginalized, the labor line running from Calalang v. Williams through eight settled doctrines, human-rights safeguards in criminal procedure, and strict death-penalty review culminating in People v. Mateo, noting his own opinion that the death penalty was unconstitutional. Conceding criticism from businessmen and a foreign diplomat, he insisted the social justice orientation must remain, lest the marginalized take the law into their own hands, and closed by quoting his book 'Leveling the Playing Field' on the Court safeguarding not only food but also freedom.
